evidence_passages.text:
**Short answer**

The conflict is real: Bun’s maintainers market it as production-ready on macOS/Linux and point to named production adopters, while multiple users report crashes, memory leaks, missing compatibility, and cases where they still keep Node in production or as a fallback. The evidence supports both of these narrower statements, but it does **not** support the strongest version of either side ("Bun is broadly proven everywhere" or "Bun is unusable in production").  
Sources: https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.0, https://bun.com/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-acquires-bun-as-claude-code-reaches-usd1b-milestone, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/25948, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/3955, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/17485

**Supported fact**

Maintainers explicitly said on September 8, 2023 that Bun 1.0 was "stable and production-ready" for macOS and Linux, while Windows was still "highly experimental" and had the package manager, test runner, and bundler disabled. https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.0

Maintainers also still say compatibility is incomplete: the docs call Node.js compatibility an "ongoing effort," and the Bun 1.4 release notes say Bun is "not 100% compatible with Node.js yet." https://bun.sh/docs, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4, https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat

Maintainers provide concrete production-use claims on the Bun homepage: it says Claude Code ships as a Bun executable, Midjourney sends every image notification through Bun’s WebSocket server, and Railway built its Functions product on Bun. https://bun.com/

Anthropic independently said on December 3, 2025 that Bun had been "key" to scaling Claude Code’s infrastructure and that Anthropic was acquiring Bun. https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-acquires-bun-as-claude-code-reaches-usd1b-milestone

The conflict is real: Bun’s maintainers market it as production-ready on macOS/Linux and point to named production adopters, while multiple users report crashes, memory leaks, missing compatibility, and cases where they still keep Node in production or as a fallback. **Supported fact**

Maintainers explicitly said on September 8, 2023 that Bun 1.0 was "stable and production-ready" for macOS and Linux, while Windows was still "highly experimental" and had the package manager, test runner, and bundler disabled. https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.0

Maintainers also still say compatibility is incomplete: the docs call Node.js compatibility an "ongoing effort," and the Bun 1.4 release notes say Bun is "not 100% compatible with Node.js yet." https://bun.sh/docs, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4, https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat

Maintainers provide concrete production-use claims on the Bun homepage: it says Claude Code ships as a Bun executable, Midjourney sends every image notification through Bun’s WebSocket server, and Railway built its Functions product on Bun. https://bun.com/

Anthropic independently said on December 3, 2025 that Bun had been "key" to scaling Claude Code’s infrastructure and that Anthropic was acquiring Bun. https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-acquires-bun-as-claude-code-reaches-usd1b-milestone

Railway independently said its Functions product runs user code on Bun, installs dependencies with `bun install`, and that Bun outperformed other package managers in its internal testing for that workflow. https://blog.railway.com/p/introducing-railway-functions

Maintainers also document concrete compatibility limits that can matter in production: `node:sea` is not implemented, Bun’s `Request` support is missing `keepalive` and `duplex`, and lifecycle scripts are blocked by default except for allow-listed or explicitly trusted packages. https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat, https://bun.com/docs/pm/lifecycle

User reports with concrete symptoms exist in Bun’s own tracker:
- An Express app in Docker was reported as crashing 4 GB pods from memory growth in production on Bun 1.2.14. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930
- A large `fetch` workload on Bun 1.2.18 was reported with RSS at 2.46 GB followed by a segmentation fault, and Bun’s own crash message said this indicated a bug in Bun. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912
- A Mongoose production build on Bun was reported as growing from about 50 MB to 170 MB in 12 hours, and another container from 300 MB to 1.5 GB in a day, even while idle, leading to container death. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/25948
- A Next.js site migration report said static generation performance was "outstanding" but also reported steadily growing memory after deploy. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/16339
- A user trying to use PM2 with Bun 1.0.0 in Docker reported a crash when invoking `bunx --bun pm2 --help`. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/4949

There are also user reports of mixed migration outcomes: one user said they migrated a monorepo with 300+ packages and about 100,000 lines of code, but hit missing APIs, memory-corruption suspicions, packaging problems, and ended up saying they still used Node "in production." https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/3955

Another user said they keep a wrapper because there are still occasions where they need to use Node "because of a bug." https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/17485

Maintainers themselves have long acknowledged reliability and depth-of-compatibility problems: Jarred Sumner wrote that Bun should not segfault, that `bun install` should work as reliably as npm, and that Bun’s Node compatibility had breadth but not enough depth. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/798

Maintainers also point to concrete remediation work in Bun 1.4: they say it adds 1,517 Node.js test-suite tests, fixes over 2,900 issues, reduces idle CPU usage by 5x, lowers memory use for HTTP-server workloads by 13% to 48% in their benchmarks, and fixes many named memory leaks and crashes. https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4

**Disagreement**

The maintainers’ public framing is: Bun is already fit for real production use on major Unix platforms, major frameworks work, and named companies are using it. https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.0, https://bun.com/, https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat

The dissatisfied-user framing is: Bun can be fast and attractive, but production workloads still surface bugs serious enough to require Node fallback, hybrid deployments, or rollback. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/16339, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/3955, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/17485

Both framings are evidenced. What conflicts is the implied generalization from each side. Sources above.

**Inference**

A reasonable inference is that Bun is credible for at least some production workloads, because Anthropic and Railway publicly describe production use and Bun’s own site names additional deployments. https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-acquires-bun-as-claude-code-reaches-usd1b-milestone, https://blog.railway.com/p/introducing-railway-functions, https://bun.com/

A separate reasonable inference is that long-running, high-load, or ecosystem-edge workloads have been a genuine reliability pain point, because Bun’s issue tracker contains repeated production-like reports of memory growth, crashes, and fallback-to-Node behavior, and Bun 1.4 devotes substantial release-note space to leak/crash fixes. https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/25948, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/3955, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4

**Uncertainty**

The issue tracker does **not** tell us prevalence. A GitHub issue proves that a user reported a concrete problem; it does not prove how common that problem is across all Bun production deployments. The same is true in the other direction: a customer quote or vendor case study proves some successful use, not broad reliability across the ecosystem. Sources: https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912, https://bun.com/, https://blog.railway.com/p/introducing-railway-functions

Some official claims are benchmark-backed but still vendor-run, not neutral third-party audits. That is true for Bun’s install/performance claims and its Bun 1.4 CPU/memory reductions. https://bun.com/, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4

**Lack of good evidence**

I did **not** find a neutral, large-scale study comparing Bun’s production incident rate against Node or Deno. I also did **not** find a rigorous public dataset showing how often Bun compatibility bugs force production rollback. The available evidence is mostly vendor documentation, release notes, product announcements, and user issue reports. Sources sampled: https://bun.com/, https://bun.sh/blog/bun-v1.4, https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions

**Bottom line**

Evidence supports this narrower conclusion: Bun is already used in production by some real organizations, and some maintainers and users report strong performance or deployment advantages. https://bun.com/, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-acquires-bun-as-claude-code-reaches-usd1b-milestone, https://blog.railway.com/p/introducing-railway-functions, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/16339

Evidence also supports this narrower conclusion: compatibility gaps and reliability bugs have been serious enough for some users to hit crashes, memory leaks, missing APIs, packaging/script issues, or continued Node fallback. https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat, https://bun.com/docs/pm/lifecycle, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/19930, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/20912, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/25948, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/3955, https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/17485

The strongest defensible summary is therefore: Bun-in-production success is evidenced, Bun-in-production pain is also evidenced, and broad claims about universal readiness or universal unreliability are not well supported by the public record above.

## Short answer

The disagreement is real, but it is **not** "maintainers say it's fine, users say it's broken." Since mid‑2026 the Bun maintainers have publicly said roughly what the harshest users said: that the runtime had a systemic memory-safety problem producing leaks and crashes. The genuine conflict is now about *scale* ("rare edge cases" vs. "unusable for long-running production") and about whether Bun's development process is trustworthy.

Below I separate what is documented from what is asserted.

---

## 1. Well-supported facts (primary sources)

**Bun's maintainers acknowledged crashes and leaks as a structural problem.** In the official post announcing the Zig→Rust rewrite, Jarred Sumner writes: *"I was tired of going to sleep worrying about crashes in Bun"*, and the post states that *"a large percentage of bugs from that list are use-after-free, double-free, and 'forgot to free' in an error path"*, attributing this to mixing JavaScript's GC with manual memory management in Zig. It cites a concrete example: a heap-use-after-free in `node:zlib` when `.reset()` is called while an async `.write()` is in flight. It also states **"Bun v1.4.0 fixes 128 bugs that reproduce in v1.3.14"** ([bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust.md)). This is the single strongest piece of evidence in the whole debate, because it is the vendor conceding the users' central complaint.

**Bun documents its own Node.js compatibility gaps, and several are production-relevant.** From [bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat):
- `node:async_hooks` — *"Bun does not invoke hooks, apart from `init` for `process.nextTick`, and async ids are always `0`"*; `AsyncLocalStorage` does not propagate into Workers or MessagePorts.
- `node:cluster` — *"implemented but not battle-tested"*; HTTP load-balancing across processes *"is only supported on Linux"* (via `SO_REUSEPORT`).
- `node:worker_threads` — ignores `resourceLimits` and `trackUnmanagedFds`; missing `moveMessagePortToContext`.
- `node:inspector` — `Runtime.evaluate` and the `HeapProfiler` domain not implemented; `node:v8` lacks `queryObjects`, `startCpuProfile`, `startHeapProfile`.
- `node:tls` — no cross-process session resumption, no OCSP stapling, no renegotiation (BoringSSL backend).
- `node:http2` — some options *"accepted but ignored"*.

This documented list is directly traceable to the most common user complaint about observability: APM/tracing agents depend on `async_hooks`, `vm` internals, and V8 profiling APIs. **Inference (mine, not documented):** the `async_hooks` and `v8` profiler gaps are a sufficient mechanical explanation for reports that tracing agents go "partially blind" and that heap profiling is hard on Bun — but I found no vendor or first-party engineering writeup confirming specific APM breakage, only third-party blog assertions.

**Bun's compatibility claim is self-measured, with stated methodology caveats.** The Bun 1.2 post says they ported thousands of Node.js test files and run them on every commit, and that *"for each of these Node modules, Bun passes over 90% of the Node.js test suite."* It also discloses adjustments: replacing *"internal bindings with our own stubs"* and relaxing assertions to check error codes rather than exact message strings ([bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2)). So the number is evidence — but it's vendor-run, on a modified suite, and per-module rather than a global figure.

**Concrete crash reports exist with real artifacts.** Issue [#31159](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/31159) reports a segfault on Bun 1.3.14 (Linux x64, Debian 13) in a Hono/`Bun.serve` SSE proxy, twice in production within an 8‑minute window on 2026‑05‑21, with stack traces pointing at `JSBytesInternalReadableStreamSource` destruction during `Response.body`/ReadableStream finalization, plus kernel "trap invalid opcode" logs and two `bun.report` links. It was closed as a duplicate. Issue [#24216](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/24216) reports steadily rising memory to OOM in a NestJS + MongoDB service on Cloud Run (512Mi), starting on upgrade from 1.2.2 → 1.2.21 and persisting on 1.3.1, with CPU/memory graphs — but the reporter himself/themselves could not produce a standalone reproduction, and the page's open/closed state was ambiguous when I read it. That caveat matters: a graph without a repro is weaker evidence than a stack trace.

**Repository scale.** [oven-sh/bun](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun) shows ~3.4k open issues, 5k+ open PRs, ~95.7k stars; the README calls Bun *"a drop-in replacement for Node.js"* and makes no explicit production-readiness declaration. A filtered query for open `crash`-labeled issues returned only 12 ([issue search](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Acrash)). **Do not read that 12 as a crash rate** — labeling is clearly inconsistent (many segfault reports found by search carry no crash label), so it's a floor, not a measurement.

**Ownership changed.** Bun was acquired by Anthropic, announced 2025‑12‑02, remaining open-source and MIT-licensed ([bun.com/blog/bun-joins-anthropic](https://bun.com/blog/bun-joins-anthropic)).

---

## 2. Where the conflict actually is

**Governance and release discipline.** In the HN thread ["I am worried about Bun"](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48011184), commenters claim Bun has *"never really been well run"*, with bugs in nearly every feature release and breaking changes shipped in patch versions; specific complaints include install freezes in large monorepos (argument buffer overflow) and `trustedDependencies` breaking without release-note mention. Jarred Sumner replied in-thread that development has *"only gotten faster"* since the acquisition, pointing to smaller binaries, HTTP/3, `Bun.Image`, and reliability work, and arguing Anthropic's incentive is aligned because *"Claude Code depends on it."* Critics in the same thread reframed that velocity as a risk, suspecting LLM-generated code and *"compounding complexity and mistakes."*

This is a genuine unresolved disagreement over interpretation of the same fact (high commit velocity). The individual bug claims (monorepo install freeze, `trustedDependencies` regression) are **unverified** — I did not locate the corresponding issues.

**"Battle-tested at scale" vs. "fails on long-running workloads."** The pro-Bun side points to large deployments; the anti-Bun side argues short benchmarks hide leaks that only long-lived processes surface. The verifiable anchor here is that the Rust rewrite post confirms Claude Code v2.1.181 (2026‑06‑17) shipped on the Rust build with ~10% faster Linux startup, and that **v1.3.14 was the last Zig release, v1.4.0 the first Rust production release** ([bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust.md)). Claims I saw that X/Twitter and Midjourney run Bun in production came only from a search summary without a citable first-party statement — treat as **unverified**.

---

## 3. Claims I found circulating that I would *not* rely on

- **Precise migration metrics** in DEV.to/Medium posts (e.g., "p50 42ms→28ms, p99 180ms→95ms, 8 engineering days," "cold start 1.8s→220ms," "~95% compatibility surface"). These are single-author, unaudited, methodologically undescribed, and mutually inconsistent. Nothing supports them beyond the author's assertion. Several of these pages have hallmarks of SEO/AI-generated content.
- **One search result described "Bun 1.1.13" as an Anthropic-era April 2026 memory-fix release.** That is internally inconsistent with Bun's own versioning (1.3.x was current in 2025–2026), so I regard those articles ([The Register](https://www.theregister.com/software/2026/04/21/bun-1113-out-with-memory-fixes-as-dev-complain-of-leaks/5221154), [DevClass](https://www.devclass.com/ci-cd/2026/04/22/anthropic-bakes-memory-fixes-into-bun-1113-as-developers-complain-of-leaks/5218433)) as unreliable as summarized and did not use them. I did not open them to adjudicate.
- **"Native addons (.node files) are not supported; sharp/bcrypt won't work."** I could not verify this either way: the Bun compatibility page I fetched had no `node:napi`/native-addon section. Given Bun has long advertised N‑API support, a blanket "not supported" is very likely wrong, but **specific package failures (e.g. `sharp`) are plausible and unverified**.
- **"99.8% test compatibility" for the Rust port** — this came from a third-party summary, not from the primary post, which instead reports 60,624 tests / 4,174 files / 1,386,826 `expect()` calls with zero tests skipped. Use the primary numbers.

---

## 4. Bottom line

The defensible statement is narrow: **through the Zig-era 1.3.x line, Bun had a documented class of memory-safety defects — acknowledged by its own maintainers — that manifested in production as leaks and segfaults, alongside documented, still-open Node.js API gaps concentrated in `async_hooks`, cluster/worker semantics, TLS, and V8 profiling.** Whether that made Bun unfit for production depends entirely on workload shape, and neither camp has published the fleet-level telemetry that would settle it. The v1.4.0 Rust release is the explicit remedy, and its real-world reliability record is **too new to have evidence yet** — the "128 bugs fixed that reproduce in 1.3.14" figure is a promising but self-reported input, not an outcome.
